analysis.title: Democratic victories to constrain President Trump and increase tech scrutiny
key_insights: Democrats won majorities in both the Senate and House in the 4 November 2026 US midterms. The Senate margin was larger than expected, with wins in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa.

Democrats lack the two-thirds supermajority needed to override vetoes. The president has said he will likely become 'Mr Veto', so spending and tax legislation is likely gridlocked. Possible compromise areas are healthcare affordability in exchange for more defence spending.

Gridlock is seen as a stable backdrop for corporate America. It also means no meaningful change to the fiscal stance, so large deficits and worsening debt dynamics continue with no further fiscal expansion.

The debt ceiling is likely to come to a head by mid-summer 2027 with little room for compromise. This risks an extended government shutdown that could exceed last October's, which cut 4Q 2025 GDP growth by a full percentage point.

Democratic control of oversight committees is likely to bring more hearings with AI and technology executives. Emboldened local Democrats may try to stall unpopular data centre construction, and fossil fuel producers may face similar challenges.

Democrats are likely to push back harder on Trump's policies on Iran, Israel support and tariff escalation. They may press him to be tougher on Russia and to support Ukraine, but the final call stays with the president.

Investigations into Trump, his family and administration are likely to increase, and impeachment proceedings would begin in the House. Conviction needs 67 senators, which is unlikely, so Democrats may target cabinet members instead.
Democrats can block or stall judicial and executive nominees in the Senate, which could make it hard for Trump to replace senior officials he fires.

With Congress gridlocked, Trump is expected to focus on executive-power areas: foreign policy and trade, national security, law enforcement and regulation, personnel and administration. Iran, Russia/Ukraine and tariffs are likely focal points, and tariffs could be used to push partners such as NATO members to raise defence spending.

Bond market reaction: yields fell across the curve initially. ING expects front-end yields to drift lower while the back end keeps an upside bias, and retains a bias towards the 10-year yield heading to 5.25%.

The dollar is softer but recovered from its early-Asia lows after a sharp drop in Nasdaq futures, which have since retraced most of their losses. A resilient US economy and at least one more Fed rate hike limit the dollar correction. More dollar weakness is possible into 2027, including from a possible mid-2027 shutdown.

For Europe, risks include a forced Russia-Ukraine deal that disadvantages Ukraine, Middle East escalation lifting energy prices, and new trade tensions. The TACO dynamic may shape European thinking, and some countries may slow defence spending increases if Trump looks weakened.

China is expected to wait and see. Trigger points are Taiwan arms sales, tariffs and trade or investment restrictions. The US-China trade truce expires in January, and neither side appears to want a return to 2025 peak tariffs, though ING says it cannot be ruled out.

sector_views.rationale: Greater congressional scrutiny is likely, with more hearings for AI and tech leaders and possible local efforts to stall data centre construction. A sharp drop in Nasdaq futures overnight pointed to a possible re-pricing of the tech story, though most of it was retraced.
Fossil fuel producers may face similar oversight and local challenges to Democrats' scrutiny of tech.

macro_indicators.interpretation: ING retains a bias towards the 10-year yield heading to 5.25%, as a still-elevated fiscal deficit keeps an upside bias at the back end of the curve.

macro_indicators.reading: at least one more rate hike
macro_indicators.interpretation: A resilient US economy and at least one more Fed hike are seen as limiting a larger dollar correction after the election.

macro_indicators.indicator: US GDP growth impact of the October 2025 government shutdown
macro_indicators.reading: depressed 4Q 2025 growth by a full percentage point
macro_indicators.interpretation: Used as the reference for the potential damage from another extended shutdown around the mid-2027 debt ceiling deadline.

risk_factors: Debt ceiling standoff by mid-summer 2027 could cause an extended government shutdown and leave the Fed without government economic statistics.
Large fiscal deficits and deteriorating debt dynamics persist with no fiscal change.
Tariff escalation could push inflation higher, offsetting the benefit of added tax revenue to the back end of the curve.
Greater scrutiny of AI and technology companies and of data centre construction.
Impeachment proceedings and investigations could further toxify the US political situation.
A constrained Trump may accept more political or market disruption in pursuit of foreign and trade objectives.
Expiry of the US-China trade truce in January could revive tariff escalation.
vol_and_positioning: Nasdaq futures fell sharply in early Asia after the results, warning of a larger re-pricing of the tech story, then retraced most of the losses.
geopolitical: Democratic Congress is likely to push back on Trump's Iran policy, support of Israel and tariff escalation.
Trump is likely to focus on Iran, Russia/Ukraine and tariffs/trade policy using executive powers. A forced Russia-Ukraine deal could disadvantage Ukraine and Europe.
A new escalation in the Middle East would push up energy prices and harm the European economy.
The US-China trade truce is set to expire in January. Possible flashpoints are Taiwan arms sales, tariffs and trade or investment restrictions.
Tariffs could be used to pressure NATO members to increase defence spending.

tension_points.bull_case: Initial reaction was a fall in yields across the curve, and easing inflation concerns from policy stasis could keep front-end yields drifting lower.
tension_points.bear_case: A still-elevated fiscal deficit with no fiscal change keeps an upside bias at the back end, and tariffs could push inflation higher.
tension_points.what_invalidates: More tariffs raising inflation, or the debt ceiling and shutdown risk by mid-summer 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: A stifled, less angry administration could try to end the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and being constrained by Congress and the Supreme Court on trade could indirectly support the European economy.
tension_points.bear_case: A constrained Trump focuses on foreign and trade policy, bringing more volatility and uncertainty for the global economy, with a risk of forced deals and escalation.
